title: Three times as wide, how heavy?
hook: Same material, three times as wide. Is it three times the weight?

knows: that area grows with the square of length (a pizza twice as wide is 4 pizzas)
doesNotKnow: that volume, and so weight, grows with the cube of length

misconception: A cube three times as wide has three times the volume, or weight (or nine times, by analogy with area).
objective: The learner can explain that scaling a solid by 3 in width also scales depth and height by 3, so its volume and weight grow 3 × 3 × 3 = 27 times.

claims.text: A 6-inch cube is filled exactly by 3 × 3 × 3 = 27 cubes of 2 inches.
claims.source: 6 / 2 = 3 cubes along each edge; 3 × 3 × 3 = 27 (recomputed in node). The stage draws k^3 unit cubes from the slider value k.

claims.text: Each small cube of the same material weighs 1 kg, so the 6-inch cube weighs 27 kg.
claims.source: Same material means the same density, so weight is proportional to volume: 27 × 1 kg = 27 kg.

claims.text: Making a solid 3 times as wide, as deep and as tall multiplies its volume by 3 × 3 × 3; 3 counts one direction and 9 counts two, which is how area grows.
claims.source: For similar solids the volume ratio is k^3 and the area ratio k^2 (e.g. any school geometry text on scale factors). Recomputed: 3, 3^2 = 9, 3^3 = 27.

claims.text: Each layer of the k-times-wide cube holds k × k small cubes, and there are k layers (stage caption, e.g. 3 layers of 9).
claims.source: Counting by z-layer: k layers of k × k = k^3. Computed in Demo.tsx from k.

recall.question: A bronze statue is copied at twice the height, same shape, same bronze. The copy needs how much bronze?
recall.why: Twice the height is also twice the width and twice the depth, so the volume is 2 × 2 × 2 = 8 times.
